subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the pinwheelImage asset with different colors in the paint editor?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What colors might you use to fill in each wedge of the pinwheel circle?

❓ What might the pinwheel and its various colors be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use a variety of colors to fill in the wedges of the pinwheel. While they can use all the different colors in the paint editor, they might consider using analogous or complementary colors to create a weaker or stronger contrast across the wheel.

💡 In this project, the pinwheel image will be used to create an animation asset. In the asset, the pinwheel will “spin” by rotating each frame to show each colored wedge in a different position.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by coloring in the pinwheel image asset. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen. 


Locate the pinWheelImage asset and notice that there are 8 transparent “wedges” of the pinwheel circle. Fill in the wedges with different colors in the paint editor.

steps.hints: ❓Did you tinker with the Interval Between Frames (ms) value in the preview animation screen on the upper right to make the pinwheel animation faster or slower?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does rotating each frame in the pinWheelAnim asset create 4 unique pixel art still images?

❓ What happens when you click on the upper right part of the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja identify the rotation tools at the top left of the animation paint editor. Make sure they have selected the correct frame so that each image is rotated 90 degrees further than the previous frame. 

💡 Point out to the ninjas that the animation paint editor has a pane on the right side with space for multiple frames of pixel art images. Above the frames, there is a play button and an Interval Between Frames (ms) value, which can be used to preview the animation and adjust how fast or slow it cycles through the frames. Point out to the ninja that this is only a preview window, meaning by viewing and tinkering with the animation in the animation paint editor, it will not change how the animation appears on the project screen.

💡 Point out to the ninja that they can select the frame they’d like to duplicate in the animation paint editor, then click Duplicate Current Frame to create a copy of the image.
steps.instructions:
Create a rotating pinwheel using multiple frames in an animation asset.


Use Ctrl + A to select, then copy the entire pinwheel image. Create a new pinWheelAnim animation asset then paste the image into the first frame in the animation paint editor.


Duplicate the first frame by clicking to create a new frame with the same image. Click “Rotate clockwise” to rotate the image 90 degrees to the right. 


Duplicate and rotate the image 2 more times, so the animation asset now has 4 total frames. 


Click to preview the animation on the upper right part of the screen as it cycles through the 4 frames of still images.

steps.hints: ❓Did you choose a background color not used in the sprite image, so that the sprite will stand out on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What color might be used for the background, so that the pinwheel sprite appears clearly?

❓ What might the frame interval be set to so that the pinwheel rotates at a proper speed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use a color not used in the pinwheel image for the background, so that the sprite appears clearly on screen.

💡 As the ninja is tinkering with the runImageAnimation code, remind them to think about the value they used in the preview window of the animation paint editor. They may choose to use the same value, or run the image animation on screen, and choose a greater or lesser value based on the rate that the animation runs.

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the documentation if they need help animating a sprite with an animation asset in their code.
steps.instructions:
Display the pinwheel sprite animation on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then set a background color that will allow the sprite to appear clearly on screen.


Create a sprite with its image set to the pinWheelImage asset. Place the sprite on the left middle part of the screen. Code the sprite to animate continuously using the pinWheelAnim asset. 


Click ▶ to test the pinwheel animation, then tinker with the frame interval value until it is rotating at a proper speed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the marquee tool to create 6 frames of progressively narrower coin images?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the coin image get progressively narrower in each frame? What effect does this have?

❓ How can the marquee tool be used to make the coin narrower in each image?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the preview window in the upper right corner of the animation paint editor to notice what happens when the frames are cycled through. The coin image gets progressively narrower, giving the effect that the coin is spinning on its side. Encourage the ninja to tinker with the frame interval to change how quickly the coin spins.

💡 Help the ninja use the marquee tool to select each side of the coin images. They might begin by clicking above the coin’s pixels on the left side, then holding the mouse down as they drag it towards the middle of the coin image. Once they’ve selected the intended area, they can move their mouse in the middle of the area to move it over by 1 pixel.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can select the frame they’d like to duplicate in the animation paint editor, then click Duplicate Current Frame  to create a copy of the image.
steps.instructions:
Create a spinning coin using multiple frames in an animation asset.

 

Open the coinImage asset. Use Ctrl + A to select, then copy the entire coin image. Create a new coinAnim animation asset then paste the image into the first frame in the animation paint editor.

 

To create an illusion of spinning, the coin image needs to gradually look more narrow to appear as if it’s turning on its side, and then expand out as it spins back around.

 

Duplicate the first frame by clicking . Use the marquee tool to select each half of the coin and drag it towards the middle, making a slightly narrower version of the coin.

 

Duplicate and edit the image 4 more times, so the coin image gets gradually narrower across 6 total frames, until it is only 1 pixel wide, showing the “edge” of the coin.

 

Click to preview the animation as it cycles through the 6 frames of still images.

steps.hints: ❓Did you duplicate frames 2-5 and drag them in reverse order so the coin appears to spin back around?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should only frames 2-5 be duplicated?

❓ What happens in the animation, after the edge of the coin is shown?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has duplicated frames 2-5 in the animation asset, then dragged them in reverse order to ensure the coin spins correctly. In the preview window, the coin should be shown at its widest point, progressively getting narrow until its narrowest point, then gradually getting wider to return to its widest point. 

💡 The frames need to be duplicated in order to show the full rotation of the coin, to mimic what the movement looks like in real life. Encourage the ninja to tinker with the frame interval to make the coin spin faster or slower.
steps.instructions:
Reuse frames to complete the spinning coin animation asset.


Duplicate and sequence the frames already created to make the coin image look like it is expanding as it completes its spin. 


Duplicate frames 2-5 of the coinAnim asset, and drag the frames in reverse order so that the images of the coin get gradually wider. 


Click to preview the animation on the upper right part of the screen as it cycles through the 10 frames of still images.

steps.hints: ❓Did you tinker with the frame interval to find the best speed for the coin animation?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the frame interval be set to so that the coin spins at a proper speed?

❓ Where might the coin sprite be placed on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 As the ninja is tinkering with the runImageAnimation code, remind them to think about the value they used in the preview window of the animation paint editor. They may choose to use the same value, or run the image animation on screen, and choose a greater or lesser value based on the rate that the animation runs.

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the documentation if they need help animating a sprite with an animation asset in their code.
steps.instructions:
Display the coin sprite animation on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then create a sprite with its image set to the coinImage asset. Place the sprite on the center part of the screen. Code the sprite to animate continuously using the coinAnim asset. 


Click ▶ to test the coin animation, then tinker with the frame interval value until it is spinning at a proper speed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you adjust the size of the animation canvas to be longer, such as 32x64, so the purple ball has room to fall and bounce?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does changing the position of the ball image in the canvas give an illusion of it falling?

❓ How can the marquee tool or Ctrl + A be used to select and move the entire ball image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 By moving the ball image a little bit lower in each frame, when the animation is run, it appears as if the ball is falling because it is lower on the canvas. 

💡 The ninja can either use the marquee tool by clicking above the left side of the ball image, then dragging their cursor to encompass the entire ball image and shifting the ball down, or use Ctrl + A to select the entire image more easily.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can select the frame they’d like to duplicate in the animation paint editor, then click Duplicate Current Frame to create a copy of the image.
steps.instructions:
Create a bouncing purple ball using multiple frames in an animation asset. 


Open the purpleBallImage asset. Use Ctrl + A to select, then copy the entire 24 x 24 ball image. Create a new purpleBallAnim animation asset. Update the canvas size so that it has room for the ball to fall down and bounce back up. Then paste the image into the first frame in the animation paint editor.


To create an illusion of falling, the different frames need to show the purple ball moving gradually from the top of the frame towards the bottom. 


Duplicate the first frame 4 times by clicking . Use the marquee tool to select the purple ball and drag it gradually lower in each frame, with the bottom edge of the ball touching the bottom of the canvas in the last frame. Click on the Show Previous Frame tool to compare the current frame with the previous frame.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the paint editor tools to stretch the purple ball by elongating it vertically, but making it narrower?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is the stretch and squash animation technique? How is it used to show the ball hitting the ground?

❓ How can the marquee tool be used to stretch the ball image, while maintaining its overall volume?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that stretch and squash is an animation technique to make movement seem more natural by elongating the moving object in the direction of the movement while keeping the total volume. It’s important to keep the overall volume the same, so that the object does not appear to get bigger or smaller. Prompt the ninja to consider what else might be added to make the ball appear to bounce on the ground, after it falls.

💡 The ball is first stretched to create an anticipation frame, or to make the next frame appear more dramatic. Work with the ninja to select the correct portions of the ball image, then rearrange them to show the ball stretched vertically.
steps.instructions:
Use the stretch technique to create the illusion that the purple ball is about to hit the ground!


Stretch and squash is an animation technique to make movement seem more natural by elongating the moving object in the direction of the movement while keeping the total volume. To create an illusion of bouncing, the purple ball needs to stretch right before it bounces, squash horizontally as it hits the floor, and stretch vertically again when it bounces up.


In the 4th frame, use the marquee tool to stretch the ball vertically by selecting the top half of the image, then dragging it towards the top to make the ball taller. 


To keep the total volume of the ball now that it is taller, the width needs to be narrower. Use the marquee tool to select each half of the ball and drag it 1 pixel towards the middle, making a slightly narrower version of the ball.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the paint editor tools to squash the purple ball to make it shorter and wider?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is the stretch and squash animation technique? How is it used to show the ball hitting the ground?

❓ How can the marquee tool be used to squash the ball image, while maintaining its overall volume?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that stretch and squash is an animation technique to make movement seem more natural by elongating the moving object in the direction of the movement while keeping the total volume. It’s important to keep the overall volume the same, so that the object does not appear to get bigger or smaller. Prompt the ninja to consider what else might be added to make the ball appear to bounce on the ground, after it falls.

💡 After the ball is stretched, it should be squashed to create the frame where the ball hits the ground. Work with the ninja to select the correct portions of the ball image, then rearrange them to show the ball squashed horizontally. Encourage the ninja to test out the animation to make sure the frames appear as expected.
steps.instructions:
Use the squash technique to create the illusion that the purple ball is hitting the ground!


In the 5th frame, use the marquee tool to squash the ball vertically by selecting the top half of the image, then dragging it towards the middle to make the ball shorter. 


To keep the total volume of the ball now that it is shorter, the width needs to be wider. Use the marquee tool to select each half of the ball and drag it 1 pixel out toward the sides, making a slightly wider version of the ball. Edit the highlight and shadow of the image as necessary. 


Click to preview the animation as it cycles through the 5 frames of still images.

steps.hints: ❓Did you duplicate frames 2-4 and drag them in reverse order so the purple ball appears to bounce back up?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

(frames 5-8)

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should only frames 2-4 be duplicated?

❓ What happens in the animation, after the ball hits the ground?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has duplicated frames 2-4 in the animation asset, then dragged them in reverse order to ensure the ball bounces back up correctly. In the preview window, the ball should be shown at its highest point, progressively getting lower (and stretched/squashed) until its lowest point when it hits the ground, then gradually getting taller as it bounces back to its highest point.

💡 The frames need to be duplicated in order to show the full bounce of the ball, to mimic what the movement looks like in real life. Encourage the ninja to tinker with the frame interval to make the ball bounce faster or slower.
steps.instructions:
Reuse frames to complete the purple ball’s bounce back up to the top of the canvas. 


Duplicate frames 2-4 of the purpleBallAnim asset, and drag the duplicated frames in reverse order so the images of the purple ball stretches, then returns to the full form and moves gradually toward the top of the canvas.


Click to preview the animation as it cycles through the 8 frames of still images.

steps.hints: ❓Did you tinker with the frame interval to find the best animation interval for the purple ball?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the frame interval be set to so that the ball bounces up and down at a proper speed?

❓ Where might the ball sprite be placed on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 As the ninja is tinkering with the runImageAnimation code, remind them to think about the value they used in the preview window of the animation paint editor. They may choose to use the same value, or run the image animation on screen, and choose a greater or lesser value based on the rate that the animation runs.

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the documentation if they need help animating a sprite with an animation asset in their code.
steps.instructions:
Display the purple ball sprite image on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then create a sprite with its image set to the purpleBallImage asset. Place the sprite on the right middle part of the screen. Code the sprite to animate continuously using the purpleBallAnim asset.


Click ▶ to test the purple ball animation, then tinker with the frame interval value until it is bouncing at a proper speed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you tinker with all 3 runImageAnimation functions and notice how the animation changes depending on the parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about each type of animation?

❓ How are the 3 animations similar? How are they different?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to look across the 3 animated sprites and notice what looks similar and what looks different. Have the ninja consider the speed of the animations, the direction that the animations are moving the sprite in, and how the animations are affecting each sprite’s movement.
steps.instructions:
Compare the 3 different types of animation!


Notice how the 3 sprites differ in how they show different types of movement. Tinker with the frame intervals and compare how the animations are similar and different!

subgroups.introduction: Practice different examples of animation techniques such as rotating, spinning, and bouncing.

validationItems.text: Use the custom animation assets to animate 3 sprites on screen.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 7 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about using still images to create animation assets. Different frames can be combined in the animation paint editor to animate a sprite’s movement in many different ways. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 7:

badges.title: I Like to Move It, Move It
badges.description: Use a variety of animation techniques to add movement to pixel art images in a project.

badges.title: Take it for a Spin
badges.description: Create animation assets that give the illusion of a sprite rotating or spinning.

badges.title: Boing!
badges.description: Create animation assets using squash and stretch that give the illusion of a sprite bouncing.

badges.title: Loafin’ Around
badges.description: Create an idle animation for a sprite.

badges.title: Frame by Frame
badges.description: Create animation assets that mimic the realistic movement of objects.

badges.title: It’s Alive!
badges.description: Use different layers to display an animation asset between 2 image assets.
